summary: Describes an optimized ingress replication solution for EVPN-based network virtualization overlays. Ingress replication avoids needing PIM in the network core but can send multiple copies of the same packet over one link; this solution reduces that cost while still not depending on PIM.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending a flyer to many houses by posting separate copies down the same street is wasteful. This reduces the wasted copies without needing special equipment.

questions: what is ingress replication in evpn
subtitle: Two tricks that let EVPN overlay networks flood broadcast and multicast traffic efficiently without running PIM in the core.

tldr.problem: Ingress replication in EVPN overlays needs no PIM in the core, but the ingress node must make a copy of every broadcast or multicast frame for each remote node, which hurts low-performance nodes such as hypervisors.
tldr.mechanism: Assisted Replication lets a weak AR-LEAF send one copy to an AR-REPLICATOR that fans it out, and Pruned Flooding Lists let nodes tell others not to send them broadcast, multicast or unknown unicast traffic. Both use new flags and a new tunnel type in the BGP PMSI Tunnel Attribute.
tldr.outcome: Networks keep the simplicity of ingress replication while cutting the replication work and the wasted copies, and nodes that do not support the new procedures keep working as regular nodes.

today: RFC 9574 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2024 and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. Its IANA section records the allocated tunnel type and flag bits.

sections.title: Ingress Replication and Its Cost
sections.content:
In a Network Virtualization Overlay (NVO) that uses EVPN as its control plane, Broadcast, Unknown Unicast, or Multicast (BUM) traffic is carried either with ingress replication (IR) or with PIM-based trees. With IR, the ingress NVE/PE makes one copy of the frame for every remote NVE/PE in the Broadcast Domain and tunnels each copy with the remote node's loopback as the outer destination address. The core just routes these packets.

PIM trees send one copy, but every router in the fabric must hold multicast state. Where the core does not support PIM, or the operator does not want it, IR is the only option. The RFC notes that IR is fine when broadcast and unknown unicast are reduced by proxy ARP/ND and control-plane MAC learning and when multicast applications are not used. When multicast sources sit on hypervisors or low-performance Top-of-Rack switches, replicating a lot of multicast to many remote nodes can seriously degrade the NVE and the application.

This document specifies two optimizations: Assisted Replication (AR) and Pruned Flooding Lists (PFLs). They can be used together or independently. Assisted Replication is aimed at NVO networks with IP tunnels; MPLS transport networks are out of scope for it, while PFLs MAY be used in both.
sections.plainLanguage: If you have to give a note to every kid in school, doing all the copying and running yourself is tiring. This document gives you two shortcuts: get a helper, and skip kids who do not want the note.

sections.title: Solution Requirements
sections.content:
The solution must reduce replication for broadcast and multicast (BM) traffic without PIM, while unknown unicast keeps following the same path as known unicast so that packets are not reordered. It must also reduce flooding toward NVEs that do not need BM or unknown unicast traffic.

It has to stay compatible with RFC 7432 and RFC 8365, including all-active and single-active multihoming and the designated forwarder function, and it has no impact on Customer Edge procedures. It must be backward compatible: one Broadcast Domain can mix NVEs/PEs with regular and optimized ingress replication. Finally, it is independent of the data plane encapsulation (VXLAN VNIs, NVGRE VSIDs or MPLS labels) as long as the tunnel is IP based.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper system must not break the old way of doing things. Kids who never heard of the new plan can still get their notes the old way.

sections.title: BGP Signaling: Roles, Flags and Routes
sections.content:
The solution reuses the EVPN Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag route and its PMSI Tunnel Attribute without changing the NLRI format. It only adds a new tunnel type and uses bits of the 1-octet Flags field. Bits 3 and 4 form the T (Assisted Replication Type) field, bit 5 is the BM flag and bit 6 is the U flag. Bits 5 and 6 are together the PFLs flags. The L flag (bit 7) is reused from RFC 6514 for selective AR.

The T field values are 00 (RNVE, no AR support), 01 (AR-REPLICATOR), 10 (AR-LEAF) and 11 (reserved; a route carrying it is treated as a Regular-IR route from an RNVE). BM = 1 means 'prune me from the BM flooding list' and U = 1 means 'prune me from the Unknown flooding list'.

Two route modes are used in a Broadcast Domain. A Regular-IR route is the ordinary ingress replication route with tunnel type 0x06; its next hop is the node's IR-IP. A Replicator-AR route is advertised by an AR-REPLICATOR with tunnel type Assisted Replication, T = 01, and a next hop called the AR-IP, which MUST differ from the IR-IP unless the single-IP procedures are followed. L is 0 for non-selective AR and 1 for selective AR. For selective AR, AR-LEAFs also use the Leaf A-D route from RFC 9572.

Non-upgraded nodes ignore the new flags and the unknown tunnel type, which is how backward compatibility works.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone puts a name tag on: helper, runner, or regular. A helper also gives out a second mailbox address that means 'please pass this along to everyone'.

sections.title: Non-selective Assisted Replication
sections.content:
Three roles exist: AR-REPLICATOR, AR-LEAF and RNVE (a regular NVE). In the non-selective mode the chosen AR-REPLICATOR replicates BM traffic to all NVEs/PEs in the Broadcast Domain except the source. BM traffic may therefore take a different path than unicast, while known and unknown unicast go directly from source to destination.

An AR-REPLICATOR MUST advertise a Replicator-AR route and MAY advertise a Regular-IR route. It checks the outer destination IP of a BM packet arriving on an overlay tunnel. If it is the IR-IP, the packet goes only to local attachment circuits (regular ingress replication). If it is the AR-IP, the node MUST replicate to local ACs and overlay tunnels, excluding the tunnel back to the source. When it sends to other replicators or leaves, the source is its IR-IP and the destination is an IR-IP, so the receiver will not replicate again.

An AR-LEAF sends all BM traffic from its ACs to one selected AR-REPLICATOR, using the AR-IP as the tunnel destination. It may pick a single replicator or load balance per flow or per BD, and SHOULD pick another if the chosen one fails. If no AR-REPLICATOR is available it MUST fall back to regular ingress replication. Service-level control packets such as IGMP, MLD and PIM use regular ingress replication. An AR-REPLICATOR-activation-timer, default 3 seconds, is RECOMMENDED so a new or rebooted replicator can program itself before leaves rely on it; during the timer the leaf uses regular IR.

An RNVE does plain ingress replication, ignores the AR routes and flags, and so interoperates unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: A weak runner gives one copy of the flyer to a helper with a fast bike. The helper delivers to everyone but the runner. If the helper is away, the runner does the rounds alone.

sections.title: Selective Assisted Replication
sections.content:
In the selective mode, an AR-REPLICATOR replicates BM traffic only to the AR-LEAFs that asked for it (and to RNVEs), so it builds multiple AR-LEAF-sets. Leaves in the same set get a single-hop tree (AR-LEAF to AR-REPLICATOR to AR-LEAF), and leaves in different sets get a two-hop tree through two replicators. The RFC says this is more efficient in multi-stage IP fabrics, at the cost of extra signaling and an additional outer source IP address lookup.

A selective AR-REPLICATOR sets L = 1 in its Replicator-AR route. If any replicator in the BD advertises L = 0, all replicators MUST fall back to non-selective behavior. A selective AR-LEAF chooses one replicator per BD, MUST send a Leaf A-D route carrying that replicator's IP-address-specific Route Target after seeing a Replicator-AR route with L = 1, and sends all BM traffic to it. It is RECOMMENDED to wait for an AR-LEAF-join-wait-timer (default 3 seconds) so it can collect all Replicator-AR routes first.

Only the first-hop replicator replicates to RNVEs, and a replicator forwards to remote replicators only when the packet came from a leaf in its own set. Mixing selective and non-selective leaves in one BD SHOULD NOT be done.
sections.plainLanguage: With several helpers, each helper only serves the kids who signed up with them, and passes the flyer to the other helpers so they can serve their own groups.

sections.title: Pruned Flooding Lists
sections.content:
With PFLs, a node signals in its Regular-IR, Replicator-AR or Leaf A-D routes that it does not want certain traffic. A node that is configured to process the flags marks the overlay tunnel to that peer. When replicating a BM packet it skips tunnels marked BM = 1, and when replicating unknown unicast it skips tunnels marked U = 1. Signaling and processing PFLs SHOULD be an administrative choice.

The RFC's example has hypervisor leaves NVE1 and NVE3 signaling BM/U = 11 because their VMs use no multicast, get ARP answered by proxy ARP on other nodes, and have their MAC and IP addresses advertised by EVPN. Then BM traffic from VM11 is not sent to NVE3, and unknown unicast from VM31 is not sent to NVE1. Nodes that do not follow this document ignore the flags, and an AR-LEAF or RNVE that receives BUM traffic on an overlay tunnel MUST still replicate it to its local ACs.
sections.plainLanguage: A friend who never reads flyers can say 'do not bother me', and you skip them. That saves you a copy and saves them from throwing it away.

sections.title: Single-IP Replicators and Multihoming
sections.content:
Normally an AR-REPLICATOR has two IP addresses, an IR-IP and an AR-IP, and the outer destination tells it which mode to use. Some software-based or low-end replicators have only one. In that case the Replicator-AR route advertises an AR-VNI different from the IR-VNI used in the Regular-IR route, the two routes need different Route Distinguishers, and the replicator picks its mode from the ingress VNI instead of the destination address.

For EVPN all-active multihoming, the split-horizon check based on tunnel source IP and local bias fails when a replicator rewrites the source to its own AR-IP. The replicator MAY therefore keep the original tunnel source IP when sending to leaves or RNVEs, but MUST use its IR-IP as source toward other replicators. If the source IP is preserved, uRPF checks based on the tunnel source in the IP fabric MUST be disabled. For MPLSoGRE or MPLSoUDP the ESI-label split horizon does not work for segments on AR-LEAF nodes, so local bias is recommended. AR-REPLICATORs sharing an all-active Ethernet Segment follow local-bias rules, and traffic that arrives with the AR-IP as destination is treated as if received on a local AC.
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper has only one phone number, the helper looks at a label on the envelope to decide whether to pass the flyer on. Twin kids who share a house must not get the same flyer twice.

sections.title: Security and Operational Risks
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7432, RFC 8365 and RFC 9572 apply. The new risks centre on BM traffic being drawn toward AR-REPLICATORs. An attack on a replicator can hurt delivery of BM traffic that uses it, and a change to the advertised AR type can alter leaf selections. If no other replicator is available, leaves are forced back to ingress replication, which hurts them because they are usually low-performance nodes.

Letting a replicator forward from one overlay tunnel to another could create BM loops. The RFC states that following its procedures prevents them, because the destination IP (or VNI) tells the next node how to forward, but an incorrect implementation may cause them. A mix of selective and non-selective replicators could duplicate packets, so the document specifies a fallback to non-selective mode. If the replicator does not preserve the leaf source IP, leaves on all-active segments cause packet duplication on the multihomed CE. Replicators use more bandwidth by design and may be overloaded, and misconfigured PFLs can leave a leaf without the traffic it needs.
sections.plainLanguage: A busy helper is a single point of trouble: if the helper is overwhelmed or tricked, many flyers go astray. So the rules include ways to avoid flyers going around in circles.

data.title: Flags octet and PMSI Tunnel Attribute fields

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Bits 3-4 are T (AR type), bit 5 is BM, bit 6 is U, bit 7 is L.

fields.name: Tunnel Type
fields.desc: 1 octet; 0x06 for ingress replication, 0x0A for Assisted Replication.

items.label: AR-REPLICATOR
items.desc: Replicates BM traffic on behalf of leaves.

items.label: AR-LEAF
items.desc: Sends BM traffic to a replicator.

items.label: RESERVED
items.desc: Treated as a Regular-IR route from an RNVE.
